title: CS1 One Ecosystem, Five Domains – Mobile 390

c.v: Medtigo’s products were built independently using different technologies and separate domains, making a technical merger impractical. I designed a shared header and navigation system to connect them into one cohesive ecosystem while allowing each platform to operate independently.
Each product runs on its own domain and its own technology.
Each product keeps its own domain and technology. Only the header is shared.
The platforms could not be technically consolidated.
Users had to understand or discover several domains to reach different products.
How a user reaches another product, before and after the shared header.
Finds or searches the URL  ·  friction
Needs another product, searches again  ·  friction
Clicks. The domain changes, the frame does not
How might we make independent products feel like one connected ecosystem without changing the technical architecture?
The constraint sits inside the question so the discussion cannot drift back to a rebuild.
Leave one layer fragmented. Unify the other two.
Five steps, from walking the products as a user to studying how other organisations solve it.
Entry points, navigation and exits, as a user would see them.
Headers, labels, logos and link behaviour across all five.
How the products relate, who owns what, and what each team needs.
Feedback, support requests and analytics, where available.
How other multi-product organisations handle navigation.
People think in goals, not domains. You find a product only if you know it exists. Consistency matters more than shared structure.
Ruled out for these constraints, not in general.
Infeasible and risky for live products.
Hidden behind a click, weak for five stable destinations.
Not where people look when they need to switch.
Looks related, but does not help anyone get anywhere.
Covers discovery, orientation and access, and any technology stack can build it.
The header is small, portable and sits in the same place on every product.
The URL changes, but the user’s mental model does not. Each item still goes to its own domain. The frame around it stays put.
Mobile, open — same items, same order, current product marked
Same position, height, labels and order on every product.
Weight and underline mark the current product. Never colour alone.
A small spec of markup, tokens and states, so no shared code is needed.
Built for every page of every product
Accessibility built into the header from the start.
A labelled navigation landmark and a skip-to-content link.
Full keyboard access in visual order, with a visible focus ring.
AA contrast targets. State is never carried by colour alone.
44px touch targets. The menu button announces expanded or collapsed.
Test with people who use more than one product. Success: no URL searching, correct “where am I” answers, easy recovery from a wrong turn.
Can people reach Courses without searching for the URL?
Can they go from Courses to Staffing in one step?
Can they get back to Home without help?
Do they know where to find the Platform?
Can they name which product they are in?
What changed and what I took from it
Design outcomes and the lessons behind them.
One navigation model across five independent products, with the technical architecture left alone.
Users no longer need to know individual URLs to move between products.
A constraint can become the brief
Fixing the experience does not always mean changing the technology.
